description: Aerobic metabolism unavoidably produces superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants, and detoxification of reactive oxygen species is the set of enzymes that converts them to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. The same chemistry sets the amplitude and duration of peroxide signalling, so these enzymes both protect cells and shape redox-sensitive responses; their failure contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegeneration, inflammation and ageing. Three superoxide dismutases act in distinct compartments — cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space — and hand hydrogen peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins. Thioredoxins and glutathione reductase, with their NADPH-dependent reductases, regenerate the reduced peroxidases each cycle. Also represented are the sources: NADPH oxidase subunits and endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductases that generate peroxide deliberately, plus copper chaperones that load superoxide dismutase with its metal cofactor.

Heme oxygenase 1 breaks down heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, and because heme is both a cofactor and a pro-oxidant, how much of this enzyme a cell makes is tightly controlled. Its induction is one of the standard cytoprotective responses to oxidative stress, hypoxia, heavy metals, inflammation and hemolysis, limiting tissue injury; loss of the enzyme in humans causes a rare syndrome of hemolysis, endothelial damage and inflammation. Control runs mainly through antioxidant response elements in the promoter, where small MAF partners such as MAFK dimerize either with NFE2L2 to drive transcription or with the heme-sensing repressor BACH1 to silence it, so that rising heme itself relieves repression. Beyond transcription, the enzyme works as a dimer anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane until the intramembrane protease HM13 releases a soluble form that reaches cytosol, mitochondria and nucleus.

Reactive oxygen species, whether generated by mitochondrial dysfunction downstream of oncogenic RAS or by prolonged interferon-beta exposure, can push a cell into an irreversible proliferative arrest, and oxidative stress induced senescence is the route by which that happens. It is a tumour-suppressive barrier: cells that sustain oxidative damage withdraw permanently from the cycle rather than propagate it, at the cost of accumulating senescent cells in ageing tissue. Oxidised thioredoxin releases MAP3K5 (ASK1), which activates the MKK3/MKK6-p38 and MKK4/MKK7-JNK arms; p38 substrates MAPKAPK2/3 and MAPKAPK5 phosphorylate BMI1 and p53 respectively, while JNK-driven AP-1 induces the H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B. Both converge on de-repression of the CDKN2A locus by evicting Polycomb complexes, raising p16INK4A to block CDK4/6-mediated RB inactivation and p14ARF to stabilise p53 against MDM2.

Cells meeting oxidative stress need NADPH, and the transcription factor NRF2 supplies it by turning up the pentose phosphate pathway. Acting with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements, and recruiting the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, NRF2 induces glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase in the oxidative branch, plus transketolase and transaldolase in the non-oxidative branch. The result reroutes glucose away from glycolysis toward NADPH production, which regenerates reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. This coupling of redox sensing to central carbon metabolism supports survival during electrophilic and oxidant challenge, and is exploited by tumours: constitutive NRF2 activation sustains the reducing power and biosynthetic precursors that proliferating cancer cells require, and contributes to chemotherapy and radiation resistance.

Cells meet heat, oxidative insult and proteotoxic stress by switching on a transcriptional programme that makes more chaperones, and the control of HSF1-mediated heat shock response determines when that switch is thrown and how quickly it is turned off again. Keeping HSF1 inactive under normal conditions matters as much as activating it: chronic activation supports tumour cell proteostasis, while blunted induction leaves neurons vulnerable to aggregated protein. HSP70 family members and their DNAJ and BAG co-chaperones bind HSF1 and hold it monomeric, a repression relieved when unfolded substrates compete for them; trimerisation, nuclear import through the nuclear pore complex with the carrier HIKESHI, and DNA binding follow. Kinases including GSK3B and the ERK1/2-MAPKAPK2 axis, together with SIRT1-dependent deacetylation and ubiquitin-mediated turnover, tune the amplitude and duration of the response.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the IRE1 arm of the unfolded protein response splices XBP1 mRNA to produce an active transcription factor, and the spliced product then drives a broad expansion of ER folding and processing capacity. This is the adaptive, pro-survival output of ER stress signalling: cells that cannot mount it fail at secretion-heavy tasks such as antibody production, insulin secretion and collagen deposition, and tip instead toward apoptosis. Spliced XBP1 binds the CCACG half of ER stress response elements together with the CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, inducing chaperones and co-chaperones (DNAJB9, DNAJB11, DNAJC3, HYOU1), oxidoreductases (PDIA5, PDIA6), degradation components for terminally misfolded substrates (EDEM1, SYVN1), translocon-associated and trafficking factors (SSR1, SERP1, SRPRA, SEC31A, KDELR3), plus WFS1, whose loss causes Wolfram syndrome.

Cells that have permanently exited the cell cycle do not fall silent; they secrete a program of cytokines, chemokines and growth-factor binding proteins known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. This secretome reinforces the arrest in the cell that makes it, recruits immune cells to clear damaged cells, and—when it persists—drives chronic inflammation, tissue ageing, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and growth of neighbouring premalignant cells. Here the transcriptional control is the focus. DNA damage signalling raises CDKN1A, which restrains CDK2 and leaves the APC/C ubiquitin ligase with its FZR1 activator competent to degrade the histone methyltransferases EHMT1 and EHMT2, de-repressing the silenced IL6 and CXCL8 promoters. Oncogenic RAS–MAPK signalling activates CEBPB, which cooperates with NF-kappa-B subunits at the same promoters, while IL6–STAT3 and IL1A feed back to sustain output. AP-1 components FOS and JUN drive IL1A and IGFBP7, and INK4/CIP-family inhibitors lock in the arrest.

The heat shock response must be switched off as well as on, and the attenuation phase is how cells terminate it once chaperone capacity again matches the load of unfolded protein. Sustained HSF1 activity is costly and, left unchecked, supports the proteostasis addiction seen in tumours, while premature shutdown leaves damaged proteins unresolved. Attenuation proceeds by several converging routes: newly made HSPA1A/HSPA1B and DNAJB1, no longer occupied by exposed hydrophobic surfaces, bind HSF1 trimers and silence them; HSP90 complexes with FKBP4 and PTGES3 favour the inactive state; HSBP1 engages the trimer and blocks DNA binding and transactivation; and acetylation by the p300/CBP acetyltransferases reduces HSF1 occupancy at heat shock elements. Trimers then leave the promoter and revert to monomers. Downstream chaperone products such as HSPB1, HSPH1 and SERPINH1 mark the response being wound down.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, one arm of the unfolded protein response cleaves ATF6-alpha and releases its cytosolic bZIP fragment to the nucleus, where it turns on the chaperone genes that restore folding capacity. This transcriptional output is what lets secretory cells such as plasma cells, hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells expand their ER and survive heavy client protein loads; when it fails, chronic ER stress pushes cells toward apoptosis. The activated fragment recognises the CCACG motif of ER stress response elements and works together with the heterotrimeric CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, whose three subunits are represented here, to drive targets including the ER chaperones BiP (HSPA5), GRP94 (HSP90B1) and calreticulin, as well as XBP1 and the stress regulators ATF4 and CHOP, linking adaptive folding capacity to cell fate decisions.

Cells that acquire a strong oncogenic signal, typically hyperactive RAS/RAF/ERK output or unrestrained E2F activity following loss of RB1, respond by permanently withdrawing from the cell cycle rather than proliferating. This oncogene-induced senescence is one of the body's first barriers to tumour formation, and its failure allows an initiating mutation to expand into a growing lesion. The response converges on the CDKN2A locus, whose two distinct products enforce arrest by separate routes: p16INK4A blocks CDK4 and CDK6 so RB1 stays hypophosphorylated and E2F target genes remain silent, while p14ARF destabilises MDM2 and thereby stabilises TP53 and its arrest programme. ERK-phosphorylated ETS1 and ETS2 drive p16INK4A transcription, ID1 opposes them, and related inhibitors including p15INK4B contribute. A microRNA-24/Argonaute arm sets a translational ceiling on both transcripts, tuning how readily cells commit to arrest.

NFE2L2 (NRF2) is the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, and how much of it a cell makes sets the ceiling on its stress defences; tumours that raise it gain resistance to oxidants and chemotherapy, while too little leaves tissues vulnerable to oxidative and electrophilic injury. Beyond the familiar control of NRF2 protein stability, transcription of the gene itself is regulated, and this is where antioxidant capacity is wired into other signalling routes. MYC, the NF- innerB subunit p65 with p50, and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, and NRF2 with its small MAF partner feeds back on its own gene, while CREBBP and EP300 supply histone acetyltransferase and coactivator function. The result couples proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to the size of the cellular antioxidant response.

The stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 (NRF2) is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also reshapes central carbon metabolism, and its control of tricarboxylic acid cycle genes is one arm of that metabolic reprogramming. Here NFE2L2 drives expression of IDH1 and ME1, two NADPH-generating dehydrogenases that link citrate and malate metabolism to reductive biosynthesis and to regeneration of glutathione and thioredoxin. The effect is to couple the cell's response to oxidative and electrophilic stress with the supply of reducing equivalents and of carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis. In tumours with constitutive NFE2L2 activation, typically through loss of its KEAP1-dependent degradation, this same wiring supports anabolic growth and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, making TCA-linked gene regulation a point where redox homeostasis and proliferative metabolism meet.

The CREB3/OASIS family of membrane-anchored transcription factors couples the secretory pathway to gene expression, allowing tissues with heavy secretory loads to expand their capacity. Each member sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane through a transmembrane segment, carrying a bZIP dimerization and DNA-binding module plus an activation domain on the cytosolic side. When these factors move to the Golgi they are cleaved in turn by the resident proteases MBTPS1 and MBTPS2, a regulated intramembrane proteolysis event that frees the cytosolic fragment to enter the nucleus and switch on target genes. Individual members act in distinct tissues: CREB3L1 in osteoblast collagen secretion, CREB3L2 in cartilage, CREB3L3 in hepatic lipid and acute-phase gene control, with CREBRF opposing this output. Several are induced by ER stress but, unlike ATF6, do not sense unfolded protein via BiP release. Loss of CREB3L1 causes osteogenesis imperfecta.

The stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also sets the tone of inflammatory gene expression, and this arm of its activity links redox state to immune signalling. Acting at antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with a small MAF partner, NFE2L2 recruits the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to remodel chromatin at target promoters, among them the monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Output is context-dependent: NFE2L2 can drive such genes directly while also restraining NF-kB-driven inflammation indirectly, partly through heme oxygenase-1. Loss of this control contributes to chronic inflammatory and oxidative-stress-associated disease, including airway and vascular inflammation, and explains why NFE2L2 activators are pursued as anti-inflammatory as well as cytoprotective agents.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, translation of the transcription factor ATF4 rises and it switches on a transcriptional programme that either restores proteostasis or commits the cell to death. This arm of the unfolded protein response, acting downstream of PERK-mediated eIF2alpha phosphorylation, drives expression of the ER-associated degradation factor HERPUD1, the amino acid biosynthetic enzyme asparagine synthetase, the growth regulator IGFBP1, the inflammatory mediators IL-8 and MCP-1, and the pro-apoptotic factor CHOP (DDIT3), with ATF3 providing feedback. ATF4 works combinatorially with C/EBP family partners and the NF-Y trimer at promoter elements, while ATF6 contributes a parallel branch. The mRNA decay machinery included here, the cytoplasmic exosome core with DIS3, deadenylases and the destabilizing factor KHSRP, sets how long these stress transcripts persist. Chronic activation contributes to secretory cell loss in diabetes and neurodegeneration.

The transcription factor NRF2 (NFE2L2) does more than defend cells against oxidative and electrophilic stress: by driving expression of drug efflux transporters it also sets how much of a xenobiotic a cell retains. This arm of its programme, in which NFE2L2 regulates multidrug resistance-associated enzymes and transporters, explains why tumours with constitutive NRF2 activity survive chemotherapy that should kill them. NFE2L2 partners with a small Maf protein such as MAFK on antioxidant response elements and recruits the coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to acetylate histones and open those promoters. Among the induced targets are ATP-binding cassette pumps: ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, and ABCG2, a broad efflux pump, alongside ABCF2, linked to platinum resistance in ovarian cancer. The same circuitry that provides cytoprotection in normal tissue therefore becomes a liability in treated cancer.

NFE2L2 (NRF2) is the transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, so how fast it is destroyed sets the cell's capacity to handle oxidative and electrophilic stress. Alongside the better-known KEAP1-CUL3 route, a second disposal route operates through the SCF ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and the substrate receptor BTRC. GSK3B phosphorylates a DSGIS motif in the Neh6 domain of NFE2L2, after priming phosphorylation of nearby serines, creating the phosphodegron that BTRC recognises; polyubiquitination then targets NFE2L2 to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Because PI3K/AKT signalling inhibits GSK3B, this branch couples growth-factor and insulin signalling to stabilised NFE2L2 and heightened stress-response output, and its loss in tumours contributes to the constitutive NRF2 activity that supports chemoresistance.

One arm of the unfolded protein response reads the folding load in the endoplasmic reticulum and answers it by making more chaperones, and ATF6B is the weaker of its two transcription factors. In resting cells ATF6B sits in the ER membrane with its lumenal domain held by the chaperone HSPA5 (BiP); when misfolded protein accumulates, HSPA5 lets go, Golgi targeting signals are exposed, and the protein moves to the Golgi. There the sequential proteases MBTPS1 (S1P) and MBTPS2 (S2P) clip it, freeing a cytoplasmic fragment carrying a bZIP domain and a nuclear localisation signal that enters the nucleus and drives chaperone and ER-quality-control genes. Because it activates transcription only weakly and heterodimerises with the stronger ATF6, it can dampen rather than amplify the response, tuning how much secretory capacity a stressed cell builds.

BACH1 is a broadly expressed transcriptional repressor that sets the threshold for the oxidative stress response: partnered with small Maf proteins such as MAFK, it occupies Maf recognition elements at antioxidant and heme-handling genes, most notably heme oxygenase-1, and keeps them silent until heme accumulates or oxidants rise. Controlling how much BACH1 protein and activity a cell carries therefore shapes redox balance, heme turnover, erythroid and immune gene programmes, and, in disease, ischemic angiogenesis and the metastatic behaviour of breast cancer cells. Regulation runs through two routes represented here. An SCF-type ubiquitin ligase built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 with the substrate receptors FBXL17 or SKP2, together with ubiquitin supplied by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal fusion precursors, marks BACH1 for proteasomal degradation. In parallel, microRNAs including miR-155 and let-7 family members limit BACH1 message output.

NRF2 is best known as the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also converges on the transcriptional arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, and this branch describes its control of ER-stress-associated targets. The central output is ATF4, a stress-induced transcription factor that lets cells survive hypoxia, amino acid limitation and accumulation of unfolded protein by turning on adaptive metabolic and chaperone genes; under sustained stress the same factor tips the balance toward apoptosis. ATF4 also drives serine and glycine biosynthesis, one reason tumour cells including non-small cell lung cancer depend on it. Transcription here requires NRF2 heterodimerised with a small MAF partner on antioxidant response elements, together with the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, linking redox sensing to proteostasis and to cancer cell stress tolerance.

Cells respond to heat, oxidants, and other proteotoxic insults by mounting the heat shock response, and HSF1 activation is the switch that turns it on. Without it, misfolded proteins accumulate unchecked and cells die under stress; constitutive activation instead supports the proteotoxic tolerance of tumour cells, making this a target in cancer. HSF1 sits in cytoplasm and nucleus as an inactive monomer held in check by chaperones including HSP90 and HSP70 family members; stress releases it, and it trimerises, accumulates in the nucleus, and binds heat shock elements to drive transcription of chaperones and co-chaperones such as DNAJB1, HSPB1, HSPH1 and ubiquitin. Feedback is built in: newly made chaperones, together with HSBP1, return HSF1 to the monomeric state, while acetylation and deacetylation, translation elongation factor and RNA-binding inputs, and RPA-mediated promoter access tune the amplitude of the response.

When reactive oxygen species or electrophiles accumulate, the transcription factor NRF2 escapes degradation, enters the nucleus and switches on a battery of cytoprotective genes; this arm of the antioxidant response is what allows cells to survive oxidative and xenobiotic insult, and its loss sensitises tissues to inflammation, chemical injury and degeneration, while its constitutive activation in tumours confers drug resistance. NRF2 binds antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins, with BACH1 acting as a competing repressor and the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 supplying coactivator function. The induced programme spans glutathione synthesis and recycling (GCLC, GCLM, GSR), cystine import through SLC7A11, glutathione transferase-mediated phase II conjugation, quinone reduction by NQO1, heme catabolism by HMOX1, and thioredoxin- and peroxiredoxin-based peroxide removal. ATF4 coupling links this response to integrated stress signalling.

Cells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage or critically short telomeres exit the cell cycle for good, and the assembly of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci is how that exit is made permanent. Each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin bearing H3K9 methylation, with telomeric and centromeric regions pushed to the periphery, and proliferation-promoting genes driven by E2F are locked in a silent state. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 stages at PML nuclear bodies before relocating to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and remodelling chromatin; linker H1 variants, HMGA proteins and loss of lamin B1 accompany the structural reorganisation. Formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, with CDKN1A enforcing the arrest. This chromatin endpoint underlies tumour suppression by senescence and contributes to the altered nuclear architecture of aged tissue.

NRF2, encoded by NFE2L2, is best known as the stress-responsive transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but when it is constitutively stabilised — as in tumours with KEAP1 loss or NFE2L2 mutation — the same factor drives a pro-tumorigenic transcriptional programme. This arm of NRF2 output supports cancer cell survival, growth-factor autonomy and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, and its activation marks aggressive lung and other epithelial cancers. Acting as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins such as MAFK and recruiting the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, with SP1 contributing to promoter occupancy, NRF2 induces anti-apoptotic BCL2 and BCL2L1, mitogens including AREG, EGF and PDGFA, and components of NOTCH1 signalling. The result couples cytoprotection to proliferation and developmental signalling, so that a defence pathway becomes a driver of tumour progression rather than a barrier to it.
